question: What information does an EU country need to share if it finds an AI system that poses a risk?
standalone_question: What information does an EU country need to share if it finds an AI system that poses a risk under the EU AI Act?
answer:
When an EU Member State finds an AI system that poses a risk, it must share the following information depending on the situation:

• For a **compliant high-risk AI system** that nevertheless presents a risk to health, safety, fundamental rights, or public interest, the Member State must immediately inform the Commission and the other Member States, including "all available details, in particular the data necessary for the identification of the AI system concerned, the origin and the supply chain of the AI system, the nature of the risk involved and the nature and duration of the national measures taken" [Art. 82(3)].

• For **non-compliance not restricted to its national territory**, the market surveillance authority must inform the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay of "the results of the evaluation and of the actions which it has required the operator to take" [Art. 79(3)].

• **Other market surveillance authorities** must, without undue delay, inform the Commission and the other Member States of "any measures adopted and of any additional information at their disposal relating to the non-compliance of the AI system concerned, and, in the event of disagreement with the notified national measure, of their objections" [Art. 79(7)].

• For AI systems **classified as non-high-risk under Annex III** where the use is not restricted to national territory, the authority must similarly inform the Commission and other Member States of the evaluation results and the actions required of the provider [Art. 80(3)].

That information shall include all available details, in particular the data necessary for the identification of the AI system concerned, the origin and the supply chain of the AI system, the nature of the risk involved and the nature and duration of the national measures taken.

question: What happens if a high-risk AI system is already being used before August 2026? Does it need to comply with the AI Act?
standalone_question: What happens if a high-risk AI system is already being used before August 2026, and does it need to comply with the AI Act?
answer:
A high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 is **not automatically subject** to the Regulation; it becomes subject only if, as from that date, it is subject to **significant changes in its design** [Art. 111(2)]. The concept of “significant change” is understood as equivalent in substance to the notion of **substantial modification** [Recital 177], which triggers a new conformity assessment procedure [Art. 43(4)].

**Exception:** Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must take the necessary steps to comply by **2 August 2030**, regardless of significant changes [Art. 111(2)] [Recital 177].

The general date of application of the Regulation is **2 August 2026** [Art. 113]. (Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)

In any case, the providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations of this Regulation by 2 August 2030.

question: What are the main rules a company has to follow if they build a high-risk AI?
standalone_question: What are the main rules a company has to follow if they build a high-risk AI?
answer:
A company building a high-risk AI system must ensure compliance with the requirements in Section 2, maintain a risk management system, and fulfill the provider obligations listed in Article 16. “Risk” means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm [Art. 3(2)].

Key rules include:

- **Compliance and risk management:** High-risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in Section 2, taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, with the risk management system referred to in Article 9 taken into account [Art. 8(1)]. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained [Art. 9(1)].

- **Quality management system:** Providers must have a quality management system in place [Art. 16(c)] that is documented systematically and includes at least: a strategy for regulatory compliance [Art. 17(1)(a)]; techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance [Art. 17(1)(c)]; and examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, with the frequency with which they have to be carried out [Art. 17(1)(d)].

- **Market and conformity obligations:** The system must undergo the relevant conformity assessment procedure prior to being placed on the market or put into service [Art. 16(f)], accompanied by an EU declaration of conformity [Art. 16(g)], CE marking [Art. 16(h)], and compliance with registration obligations [Art. 16(i)].

- **Documentation and information:** Providers must indicate their name, registered trade name or trademark and contact address [Art. 16(b)], keep technical documentation [Art. 16(d)], keep logs when under their control [Art. 16(e)], take necessary corrective actions and provide information as required [Art. 16(j)], demonstrate conformity upon reasoned request of a national competent authority [Art. 16(k)], and ensure compliance with accessibility requirements [Art. 16(l)].

question: When is a high-risk AI assumed to meet the relevant requirements?
standalone_question: When is a high-risk AI system presumed to be in conformity with the relevant requirements under the EU AI Act?

question: If a high-risk AI system is changed or keeps learning after launch, does it need a new assessment?
standalone_question: If a high-risk AI system is changed or keeps learning after launch, does it need a new conformity assessment under the EU AI Act?
answer:
It depends on whether the change constitutes a “substantial modification”:

• **Substantial modification → new conformity assessment required.** A high-risk AI system that has already undergone a conformity assessment must undergo a **new conformity assessment** in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer [Art. 43(4)]. A change that may affect compliance (e.g., a change of operating system or software architecture) or a change in the intended purpose is treated as making the system a new AI system that should undergo a new conformity assessment [Recital 128].

• **Exception for continuing learning.** For high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, changes to the system and its performance that were **pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment** and are part of the technical documentation **do not constitute a substantial modification** and therefore do not trigger a new conformity assessment [Art. 43(4)]; likewise, changes to the algorithm and performance of systems that continue to learn are not substantial modifications provided they were pre-determined and assessed at the conformity assessment [Recital 128].

• **Process for other changes.** Any change that could affect compliance or the intended purpose must be assessed by the notified body: the provider must inform the notified body of its intention to introduce such changes, and the notified body decides whether those changes require a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4) or can be addressed by a supplement to the certificate [Annex VII, points 4–5].

question: How do companies put human oversight in place for a high-risk AI?
standalone_question: How do companies put human oversight in place for a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Companies put human oversight in place for high-risk AI systems through the following requirements:

**Design and purpose**
High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed with appropriate human-machine interface tools so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during use [Art. 14(1)]. Human oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, especially when such risks persist despite other requirements [Art. 14(2)].

**Types of oversight measures**
Oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, ensured through either: (a) measures built into the system by the provider before placing it on the market, or (b) measures identified by the provider and implemented by the deployer [Art. 14(3)].

**Capabilities of oversight persons**
The system must be provided so that assigned natural persons can: (a) understand its capacities and limitations and monitor its operation; (b) remain aware of automation bias; (c) correctly interpret the output; (d) decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output; and (e) intervene or interrupt the system via a 'stop' button or similar procedure [Art. 14(4)].

**Deployer obligations**
Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training, authority and support [Art. 26(2)]. The instructions for use provided to deployers must contain information on the human oversight measures, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs [Art. 13(3)(d)].

**Special verification requirement**
For high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, point 1(a), no action or decision may be taken based on the system’s identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (with an exception for certain law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum uses where Union or national law deems the requirement disproportionate) [Art. 14(5)].

**Ongoing monitoring**
Providers must maintain a post-market monitoring system as part of their quality management system [Art. 17(1)(h)].

They can be built into the system by the provider before it is placed on the market or put into service, when technically feasible. Alternatively or additionally, the provider can identify measures beforehand that are appropriate for the deployer to implement.

question: Are the organizations that check high-risk AI systems allowed to share the information they see during an assessment?
standalone_question: Are the organizations that check high-risk AI systems allowed to share the information they see during an assessment according to the EU AI Act?
answer:
Generally no: notified bodies must keep confidential the information they obtain during conformity assessment activities, with only specific exceptions.

They must maintain confidentiality of information coming into their possession during conformity assessment activities “except when its disclosure is required by law,” and their staff are bound by professional secrecy “except in relation to the notifying authorities” [Art. 31(7)]. They must also “safeguard the confidentiality of the information that they obtain, in accordance with Article 78” [Art. 45(4)], and Article 78(1) requires notified bodies to respect confidentiality so as to protect, in particular, intellectual property rights, confidential business information or trade secrets, effective implementation of the Regulation, public and national security interests, proceedings, and classified information [Art. 78(1)].

The specific sharing that is allowed/required is limited: notified bodies must inform the notifying authority of certificates, refusals/restrictions/suspensions/withdrawals, circumstances affecting notification, requests from market surveillance authorities, and, on request, conformity assessment activities performed [Art. 45(1)], and they must provide other notified bodies covering the same types of AI systems with relevant information on negative and, on request, positive conformity assessment results [Art. 45(3)].

Notified bodies shall have documented procedures in place ensuring that their personnel, committees, subsidiaries, subcontractors and any associated body or personnel of external bodies maintain, in accordance with Article 78, the confidentiality of the information which comes into their possession during the performance of conformity assessment activities, except when its disclosure is required by law. The staff of notified bodies shall be bound to observe professional secrecy with regard to all information obtained in carrying out their tasks under this Regulation, except in relation to the notifying authorities of the Member State in which their activities are carried out.
reference_answer_generated: Notified bodies must have documented procedures to ensure that their staff, subcontractors, and associated bodies maintain the confidentiality of information obtained during conformity assessment activities, unless disclosure is required by law. Their staff must also observe professional secrecy regarding all information obtained in their tasks, except in relation to the notifying authorities of the Member State where they operate.

question: What happens when a notified body's notification needs to be changed or expanded?
standalone_question: What happens when a notified body's notification needs to be changed or expanded under the EU AI Act?
answer:
When a notified body's notification changes, the notifying authority must notify the Commission and the other Member States of any relevant changes via the electronic notification tool [Art. 36(1)]. The procedure depends on the nature of the change: for **extensions of the scope** of the notification, the procedures laid down in Articles 29 and 30 apply, whereas for **other changes**, the procedures in paragraphs (3) to (9) of Article 36 apply [Art. 36(2)]. Additionally, the notified body must update its documentation whenever relevant changes occur to enable monitoring of continuous compliance [Art. 29(4)].

If the change involves the **restriction, suspension, or withdrawal of the designation**, the notifying authority must assess the impact on certificates, submit a report within three months, require the suspension or withdrawal of unduly issued certificates, and inform the Commission, Member States, and the relevant national competent authority [Art. 36(7)]. The notified body must inform affected providers within 10 days [Art. 36(5)], and the notifying authority must ensure the body's files are kept and made available to other notifying and market surveillance authorities [Art. 36(6)]. Certificates (except unduly issued ones) may remain valid under specific conditions during suspension or restriction [Art. 36(8)], or for nine months (extendable in three-month periods up to 12 months total) upon withdrawal if another notified body assumes responsibility and no risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights is confirmed [Art. 36(9)].

question: If a company uses an AI system to make a decision that negatively affects my rights, can I ask for an explanation?
standalone_question: If a company uses an AI system to make a decision that negatively affects my rights, can I ask for an explanation under the AI Act?
answer:
Yes, you may have the right to obtain an explanation, provided specific conditions are met.

Under Article 86(1), you have the right to obtain from the deployer “clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken” if: (1) the decision is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a **high-risk AI system listed in Annex III** (except systems listed under point 2 thereof), and (2) that decision “produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights” [Art. 86(1)].

This right does not apply where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law [Art. 86(2)], and it applies only to the extent that such a right is not otherwise provided for under Union law [Art. 86(3)]. The right is intended to provide a basis on which affected persons can exercise their rights [Recital 171].

question: What happens if an authority thinks a company's AI system is actually high-risk even though the company said it wasn't?
standalone_question: What happens if an authority considers a company's AI system to be high-risk even though the company classified it otherwise under the EU AI Act?
answer:
If a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider that an AI system classified by the provider as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) is indeed high-risk, the authority shall carry out an evaluation of the system's classification based on the conditions set out in Article 6(3) and the Commission guidelines [Art. 80(1)].

If that evaluation finds the system is high-risk, the authority shall without undue delay require the provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with the Regulation and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe [Art. 80(2)]. The provider must ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market [Art. 80(5)].

Where the use of the system is not restricted to the authority's national territory, the authority shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay of the results of the evaluation and of the actions required [Art. 80(3)].

If the provider does not take adequate corrective action within the prescribed period, Article 79(5) to (9) shall apply [Art. 80(6)]. If the authority establishes that the system was misclassified as non-high-risk in order to circumvent the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, the provider shall be subject to fines in accordance with Article 99 [Art. 80(7)].

Separately, a provider who considers an Annex III system not high-risk must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, be subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and provide that documentation to national competent authorities upon request [Art. 6(4)].

question: What details about how an AI system was built and designed need to be included in the technical documentation under Annex IV point 2?
standalone_question: What details about how an AI system was built and designed need to be included in the technical documentation under Annex IV point 2 of the EU AI Act?
answer:
Under Annex IV, point 2, the technical documentation must include the following details about the AI system’s development and design:

• **Development methods and steps**: the methods and steps performed for development, including any recourse to pre-trained systems or tools provided by third parties and how those were used, integrated or modified [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Design specifications**: the general logic and algorithms; key design choices including rationale and assumptions made; the persons or groups of persons the system is intended for; main classification choices; what the system is designed to optimise for and the relevance of parameters; expected output and output quality; and any trade-offs made regarding technical solutions to comply with Chapter III, Section 2 [Annex IV, point 2].

• **System architecture and computational resources**: how software components build on or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing; and the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate the system [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Data requirements**: datasheets describing training methodologies, techniques and training data sets used, including their provenance, scope and main characteristics; how the data was obtained and selected; labelling procedures; and data cleaning methodologies [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Human oversight assessment**: an assessment of the human oversight measures needed under Article 14, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs by deployers under Article 13(3)(d) [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Pre-determined changes**: where applicable, a detailed description of pre-determined changes to the system and its performance, together with technical solutions to ensure continuous compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Validation and testing**: procedures used, including validation and testing data and their main characteristics; metrics used to measure accuracy, robustness, compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 and potentially discriminatory impacts; and dated, signed test logs and reports [Annex IV, point 2].

• **Cybersecurity**: the cybersecurity measures put in place [Annex IV, point 2].

question: Can police use personal data in an AI testing space to help fight crime?
standalone_question: Can police use personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox or testing space to help fight crime under the EU AI Act?

question: What general rules apply to the CE marking for high-risk AI systems?
standalone_question: What general rules apply to the CE marking for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act?

The CE marking for high-risk AI systems must follow the general principles set out in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 [Art. 48(1)], and indicates that the system is in conformity with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 and other applicable Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 3(24)]. Providers must affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation [Art. 16].

Key rules include:

- It must be affixed **visibly, legibly and indelibly**; where this is not possible or warranted due to the nature of the system, it must be affixed to the packaging or accompanying documentation [Art. 48(3)].
- For high-risk AI systems **provided digitally**, a **digital CE marking** must be used, accessible via the interface or an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means [Art. 48(2)].
- Where applicable, it must be followed by the **identification number of the notified body** responsible for the conformity assessment; this number must also appear in promotional material stating the system fulfils CE marking requirements [Art. 48(4)].
- Where the system is subject to **other Union law** also requiring CE marking, the marking indicates compliance with those requirements as well [Art. 48(5)].

question: What do companies that build general-purpose AI models have to do under the rules?
standalone_question: What are the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
Providers of general-purpose AI models—defined as models displaying significant generality capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks that can be integrated into various downstream systems, except those used for research, development or prototyping before placing on the market [Art. 3(63)]—must fulfill the following obligations:

**Core obligations under Article 53(1):**
*   Draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation of the model (including training/testing processes and evaluation results) containing at minimum the information in Annex XI, to provide upon request to the AI Office and national competent authorities [Art. 53(1)(a)];
*   Draw up, keep up-to-date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems integrating the model, enabling them to understand its capabilities and limitations and comply with their obligations, containing at minimum the elements in Annex XII [Art. 53(1)(b)];
*   Put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, in particular to identify and comply with reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [Art. 53(1)(c)];
*   Draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content according to the AI Office template [Art. 53(1)(d)].

**Cooperation and compliance:**
*   Cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences [Art. 53(3)];
*   May rely on codes of practice or European harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1) obligations, or otherwise demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment [Art. 53(4)].

**Additional obligations for models with systemic risk (Article 55(1)):**
In addition to Articles 53 and 54, providers must: perform model evaluation including adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [Art. 55(1)(a)]; assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level [Art. 55(1)(b)]; keep track of, document and report serious incidents without undue delay to the AI Office and national authorities [Art. 55(1)(c)]; and ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure [Art. 55(1)(d)].

**Exception for open-source models:**
The obligations in points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1) do not apply to providers releasing models under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture and usage information, except for general-purpose AI models with systemic risks [Art. 53(2)].

**Confidentiality:**
Any information or documentation obtained pursuant to Article 53, including trade secrets, shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations in Article 78 [Art. 53(7)].

They also need to implement a policy to comply with EU copyright law and publish a detailed summary of the content used to train the model.

question: What rules apply to the quality of data used to build and test high-risk AI?

Those data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose [Art. 10(3)]. They must have appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used; these characteristics may be met at the level of individual data sets or a combination thereof [Art. 10(3)]. For high-risk AI systems not using training techniques, these requirements apply only to the testing data sets [Art. 10(6)].

Procedurally, providers must document a quality management system that includes systems and procedures for data management—covering data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, data mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before placing on the market [Art. 17(1)(f)]—as well as examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development [Art. 17(1)(d)].

question: What factors do authorities look at when deciding how big a fine to give for breaking the AI rules?
standalone_question: What factors do authorities look at when deciding how big a fine to give for breaking the rules of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
When deciding whether to impose an administrative fine and determining its amount, authorities must take into account all relevant circumstances of the specific situation [Art. 99(7)]. The key factors include:

**General factors for operators [Art. 99(7)]:**
- The nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, including the purpose of the AI system, the number of affected persons and the level of damage suffered [Art. 99(7)(a)]
- Whether fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities or other authorities to the same operator for the same or related infringements [Art. 99(7)(b), Art. 99(7)(c)]
- The size, annual turnover and market share of the operator [Art. 99(7)(d)]
- Aggravating or mitigating factors such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided from the infringement [Art. 99(7)(e)]
- The degree of cooperation with national competent authorities to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects [Art. 99(7)(f)]
- The degree of responsibility based on technical and organisational measures implemented [Art. 99(7)(g)]
- How the infringement became known, particularly whether the operator notified it [Art. 99(7)(h)]
- Whether the infringement was intentional or negligent [Art. 99(7)(i)]
- Any action taken to mitigate harm to affected persons [Art. 99(7)(j)]

**For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies [Art. 100(1)]:** authorities consider similar factors including the nature and gravity of the infringement, degree of responsibility, cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor, previous infringements, how the infringement became known, and the annual budget of the entity [Art. 100(1)(a)-(g)].

**For providers of general-purpose AI models [Art. 101(1)]:** the Commission considers the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement with due account of proportionality and appropriateness, as well as any commitments made under Article 93(3) or relevant codes of practice [Art. 101(1)].

They also look at the operator's size, annual turnover, and market share, whether the infringement was intentional or negligent, and how much the operator cooperated or tried to reduce the harm. Additionally, they take into account any previous fines for the same issue, any financial benefits gained, and how the authorities found out about the violation.

question: Are open-source AI tools covered by the EU AI rules?
standalone_question: Are open-source AI tools covered by the EU AI Act?
answer:
Open-source AI tools are generally excluded from the scope of the EU AI Act, but this exclusion is subject to specific exceptions and conditions.

Under [Art. 2(12)], the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, **unless** they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50.

For general-purpose AI models, the obligations for providers and authorised representatives do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, usage, modification, and distribution, provided the parameters (including weights, model architecture, and usage information) are made publicly available; however, this exception **does not apply** to models with systemic risks [Art. 53(2)] [Art. 54(6)].

Regarding the AI value chain, the requirement for a written agreement with third-party suppliers does not apply to third parties making tools, services, processes, or components (other than general-purpose AI models) publicly accessible under a free and open-source licence [Art. 25(4)].

Nevertheless, [Recital 103] clarifies that AI components provided against a price or otherwise monetised—including through technical support, platform services, or the use of personal data for reasons other than security, compatibility, or interoperability (with an exception for transactions between microenterprises)—should **not** benefit from the free and open-source exceptions.

question: If an AI creates fake images, videos, or text, do the makers have to mark them as AI-generated?
standalone_question: Under the EU AI Act, do providers of AI systems that generate deepfakes, text, images, videos, or audio have to label or mark them as AI-generated?
answer:
Yes. Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure that the outputs are “marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated,” with technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible [Art. 50(2)]. This obligation does not apply where the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or semantics, or where use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences [Art. 50(2)].

For deep fakes specifically, the disclosure obligation falls on deployers rather than providers: deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake (defined as content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic [Art. 3(60)]) must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, with limited exceptions for artistic, creative, satirical, fictional works [Art. 50(4)]. Similarly, deployers must disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has undergone human review with editorial responsibility held by a natural or legal person [Art. 50(4)]. Recital 133 confirms that providers should embed technical solutions such as watermarks, metadata or cryptographic methods to enable this marking [Recital 133].

question: Does the AI Act override existing EU rules that protect consumers and keep products safe?
standalone_question: Does the AI Act override existing EU rules that protect consumers and keep products safe?
answer:
No. The AI Act does not override existing EU consumer protection and product safety rules; it applies alongside them.

The Act expressly states that it is “without prejudice to the rules laid down by other Union legal acts related to consumer protection and product safety” [Art. 2(9)]. Recital 9 confirms that the harmonised rules are “without prejudice to existing Union law, in particular on … consumer protection … and product safety, to which this Regulation is complementary,” and that rights and remedies under such laws “remain unaffected and fully applicable” [Recital 9]. For AI systems that are not high-risk, existing product safety law still applies as a “safety net” [Recital 166].

question: What happens to my AI system's certificate if the body that issued it loses its designation?
standalone_question: What happens to an AI system's certificate if the notified body that issued it loses its designation under the EU AI Act?
answer:
If a notified body loses its designation, the fate of the certificates depends on whether the designation is suspended/restricted, withdrawn, or the body ceases its activities:

**Suspension or restriction** — Certificates remain valid (except those unduly issued) if the notifying authority confirms within one month that there is no risk to health, safety or fundamental rights and outlines a remedy timeline, or if it confirms no new certificates will be issued and the notified body confirms it can still monitor existing certificates; if the notified body cannot support existing certificates, the provider must confirm in writing within three months that another qualified notified body is temporarily assuming those functions [Art. 36(8)].

**Withdrawal** — Certificates remain valid for nine months if the national competent authority confirms there is no risk to health, safety or fundamental rights and another notified body confirms in writing that it assumes immediate responsibility and will complete its assessment within 12 months; the national authority may extend this validity in additional three-month periods up to 12 months total [Art. 36(9)].

**Cessation of activities** — Certificates may remain valid for nine months after the notified body ceases activities, provided another notified body confirms in writing it will assume responsibility and completes a full assessment within that nine-month period before issuing new certificates [Art. 36(3)].

In all cases, the notifying authority must assess the impact on certificates, report to the Commission and other Member States within three months, and require suspension or withdrawal of any unduly issued certificates [Art. 36(7)]. The affected notified body must also inform the providers concerned within 10 days [Art. 36(5)].

question: If I use third-party tools or components in my high-risk AI system, do I need a contract with the supplier, and what if they are open-source?

Yes. If a third party supplies an AI system, tools, services, components, or processes that are used or integrated in your high-risk AI system, you must have a written agreement specifying the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance, based on the generally acknowledged state of the art, so you can comply with the Regulation [Art. 25(4)]. The rationale is that these third parties play an important role and should provide that assistance without compromising their IP or trade secrets [Recital 88].

Separately, free and open-source AI systems are generally outside the Regulation’s scope unless they are high-risk or fall under Article 5 or 50 [Art. 2(12)].

question: What happens if an AI system stops meeting the requirements after it has been certified?
standalone_question: What happens under the EU AI Act if an AI system stops meeting the requirements after it has been certified or placed on the market?
answer:
If a certified high-risk AI system stops meeting the requirements, the notified body may **suspend or withdraw the certificate or impose restrictions**, unless the provider takes appropriate corrective action within a deadline set by the notified body; the notified body must give reasons for its decision, and an appeal procedure is available [Art. 44(3)].

Where a market surveillance authority finds that an AI system (classified by the provider as non-high-risk under Annex III) is in fact high-risk, it must require the provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance and take appropriate corrective action within a prescribed period [Art. 80(2)]. If the provider fails to bring the system into compliance within that period, the provider is subject to fines under Article 99 [Art. 80(4)], and must ensure appropriate corrective action for all concerned systems made available on the Union market [Art. 80(5)].

If the non-compliance of a high-risk AI system persists, the market surveillance authority must take appropriate and proportionate measures to restrict or prohibit the system being made available on the market, or ensure it is recalled or withdrawn without delay [Art. 83(2)].

Additionally, if the system undergoes a **substantial modification** after its conformity assessment, it must undergo a new conformity assessment procedure, regardless of whether it is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer (changes that were pre-determined at the initial assessment do not constitute a substantial modification) [Art. 43(4)].

question: What should I check when preparing and managing data for a high-risk AI?
standalone_question: What are the requirements for data governance and data management when preparing data for a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
For high-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models, training, validation and testing data sets must meet the quality criteria in paragraphs 2 to 5 of Article 10 whenever such data sets are used [Art. 10(1)]. For high-risk AI systems not using training techniques, paragraphs 2 to 5 apply only to the testing data sets [Art. 10(6)].

**Quality criteria for the data sets**
Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with appropriate statistical properties regarding the persons or groups of persons for whom the system is intended [Art. 10(3)]. Data sets shall also take into account the characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the system is intended to be used [Art. 10(4)].

**Data governance and management practices**
These practices must concern in particular: (a) relevant design choices; (b) data collection processes, origin of data and, for personal data, the original purpose of collection; (c) data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; (d) formulation of assumptions about what the data measure and represent; (e) assessment of availability, quantity and suitability of needed data sets; (f) examination for possible biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights or leading to prohibited discrimination; (g) appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate identified biases; and (h) identification of data gaps or shortcomings and how to address them [Art. 10(2)].

**Special categories of personal data**
To the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under paragraph 2(f) and (g), providers may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only if: (a) bias detection cannot be fulfilled with other, synthetic or anonymised data; (b) data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures including pseudonymisation; (c) data are secured with strict access controls and documentation; (d) data are not transmitted or accessed by other parties; (e) data are deleted once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends; and (f) processing records include the reasons why special category data were strictly necessary [Art. 10(5)].

**Quality management system**
Providers must document systems and procedures for data management—including acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and other operations performed before placing on the market or putting into service—within their quality management system [Art. 17(1)(f)].

These practices include reviewing design choices, data collection processes, data preparation, and the availability and suitability of the data. They also require checking for and mitigating possible biases, as well as identifying and addressing any data gaps or shortcomings.

question: What counts as an AI system under the EU AI Act?
standalone_question: What counts as an AI system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
An **AI system** is a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, possibly exhibiting adaptiveness after deployment, that infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments [Art. 3(1)].

Key characteristics that distinguish AI systems from simpler traditional software include:

*   **Capability to infer**: the process of obtaining outputs and deriving models or algorithms from inputs or data, which transcends basic data processing by enabling learning, reasoning or modelling; this excludes systems based solely on rules defined by natural persons to automatically execute operations [Recital 12].
*   **Machine-based**: the system runs on machines [Recital 12].
*   **Objectives**: it operates for explicit or implicit objectives, which may differ from its intended purpose in a specific context [Recital 12] [Art. 3(1)].
*   **Autonomy and adaptiveness**: it has some degree of independence from human involvement and, after deployment, may exhibit self-learning capabilities that allow it to change while in use [Recital 12].

A **general-purpose AI system** is also an AI system: it is based on a general-purpose AI model and has the capability to serve a variety of purposes, either for direct use or for integration into other AI systems [Art. 3(66)].

question: What does market surveillance authority mean in the AI Act?

*   For high-risk AI systems used by financial institutions regulated by Union financial services law, it is the relevant national authority responsible for financial supervision of those institutions; another authority may be designated by derogation if coordination is ensured [Art. 74(6)], [Art. 74(7)].

*   For Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies within the scope of the Regulation, it is the European Data Protection Supervisor, except for the Court of Justice of the European Union acting in its judicial capacity [Art. 74(9)].

question: What is an AI regulatory sandbox in the AI Act?

question: What counts as a substantial modification to an AI system under the AI Act?
standalone_question: What counts as a substantial modification to an AI system under the AI Act?
answer:
A **substantial modification** is a change to an AI system after its placing on the market or putting into service which is **not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment** and as a result of which **compliance with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 is affected** or which **results in a modification to the intended purpose** for which the system was assessed [Art. 3(23)].

However, for high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, changes to the system and its performance that were **pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment** and are part of the technical documentation **do not constitute a substantial modification** [Art. 43(4)]. Recital 128 confirms that changes affecting compliance (e.g., change of operating system or software architecture) or the intended purpose trigger a new conformity assessment, while pre-determined learning changes are excluded [Recital 128].

question: What is the AI Office in the EU AI Act?
standalone_question: What is the AI Office in the EU AI Act?
answer:
The AI Office is the Commission’s function of contributing to the implementation, monitoring and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, and AI governance, as provided for in the Commission Decision of 24 January 2024; references to the AI Office are construed as references to the Commission [Art. 3(47)]. The Commission develops Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [Art. 64(1)], and Member States must facilitate the tasks entrusted to it [Art. 64(2)].

Its tasks include providing the secretariat for the European Artificial Intelligence Board, convening its meetings and preparing the agenda [Art. 65(8)]; monitoring and supervising compliance of AI systems based on general-purpose AI models where the model and system are developed by the same provider, with all the powers of a market surveillance authority [Art. 75(1)]; encouraging and facilitating the review and adaptation of codes of practice and assisting in the assessment of available standards [Art. 56(8)]; and undertaking actions such as providing standardised templates, developing a single information platform, organising awareness campaigns, and evaluating best practices in public procurement of AI systems [Art. 62(3)]. By 2 August 2028, the Commission must evaluate whether the AI Office has sufficient powers and competences to fulfil its tasks and whether it should be upgraded [Art. 112(5)].

Before that, the Member State must lay down in its national law detailed rules for the request, issuance, exercise, supervision and reporting of authorisations, specifying the relevant law-enforcement objectives and competent authorities [Art. 5(5)]. Member States may also introduce more restrictive laws [Art. 5(5)].

For each individual use of the system, the following steps apply: a prior authorisation must be obtained from a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, except in a duly justified situation of urgency, where authorisation may be requested without undue delay and at the latest within **24 hours**; if rejected, use must stop immediately and data deleted [Art. 5(3)]. The deployer must also complete a fundamental rights impact assessment and register the system in the EU database (though registration may be completed without undue delay in urgent cases) [Art. 5(2)], and each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and national data protection authority [Art. 5(4)].

question: We are a consumer advocacy group worried that future updates to the rules for deciding which AI systems are high-risk might weaken protections for people. Are there limits on how those rules can be changed?

answer:
Yes. Amendments to the high-risk classification rules are subject to specific limits:

*   **No decrease in protection:** Any amendment to the conditions in Article 6(3) "shall not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation" [Art. 6(8)]. Similarly, removing an AI system from Annex III is only permitted where "the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under Union law" [Art. 7(3)(b)].
*   **Consistency and context:** Such amendments must "ensure consistency with the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Article 7(1)" and "take account of market and technological developments" [Art. 6(8)].
*   **Evidence requirement:** The Commission may only add, modify, or delete conditions in Article 6(3) where there is "concrete and reliable evidence" of the relevant risk situation [Art. 6(6)] [Art. 6(7)].

question: We are a software company about to launch a high-risk AI tool in the EU. What contact details and markings do we need to include on the product or its packaging?
standalone_question: What contact details and markings do software companies need to include on a high-risk AI tool or its packaging to comply with the EU AI Act?
answer:
Providers of a high-risk AI system must indicate on the system itself or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation, their **name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted** [Art. 16]. Importers must likewise indicate their own **name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and contact address** on the system, its packaging or accompanying documentation [Art. 23(3)].

For markings, the **CE marking** must be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly to the high-risk AI system; if that is not possible or not warranted because of the system’s nature, it must be affixed to the packaging or accompanying documentation [Art. 48(3)]. Where applicable, the CE marking must be followed by the **identification number of the notified body** responsible for the conformity assessment, affixed by that body or under its instructions by the provider or authorised representative, and the same number must appear in any promotional material stating that the system fulfils CE-marking requirements [Art. 48(4)].

In addition, the instructions for use must contain the **identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative** [Art. 13(3)(a)].

question: We are a start-up building an AI tool that acts as a safety part in medical devices, which already need an outside check before being sold. Does that mean our AI is automatically treated as high-risk?

question: I run a company and want to use software that analyzes our employees' facial expressions during meetings to see how they feel about new projects. Is this allowed?

question: Our company is planning to use a high-risk AI tool, and we need to do a privacy assessment under EU data protection law. Can we use the documentation the AI vendor gave us to help with that?

question: Our company uses a high-risk AI tool to help us decide which job applicants to interview. Do we have to tell the applicants that we are using this system?

question: We are a start-up building an AI image generator, and we're unsure how to handle the rules for labelling synthetic content. Will there be EU-wide guidelines to help us, or can the European Commission just set mandatory rules?
standalone_question: What are the rules for labelling synthetic content generated by AI, and will there be EU-wide guidelines or mandatory rules set by the European Commission?
answer:
Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure their outputs are **marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated**, using technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible [Art. 50(2)]. This does not apply where the system performs an assistive editing function, does not substantially alter input data, or where use is authorised by law for law enforcement [Art. 50(2)].

Deployers face specific disclosure duties: they must disclose that deep fake content—defined as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic [Art. 3(60)]—has been artificially generated or manipulated [Art. 50(4)]. Exceptions apply for law enforcement and for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works, where disclosure is limited to an appropriate manner that does not hamper the work’s display [Art. 50(4)]. Deployers must also disclose when AI-generated text is published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless authorised by law for criminal proceedings or where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility [Art. 50(4)].

Regarding EU-wide guidance and mandatory rules: the Commission **shall develop guidelines** on the practical implementation of the transparency obligations laid down in Article 50 [Art. 96(1)]. Additionally, the AI Office shall encourage and facilitate **codes of practice at Union level** for the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content [Art. 50(7)], [Recital 135]. The Commission may adopt implementing acts to approve such codes, or, if a code is deemed inadequate, adopt implementing acts specifying **common mandatory rules** for these obligations [Art. 50(7)].

If it deems the code is not adequate, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for the implementation of those obligations in accordance with the examination procedure laid down in Article 98(2).

question: My company is about to start using a high-risk AI tool for screening job applicants. What do we need to do to make sure we are using it properly?

Deployers of high-risk AI systems used for screening job applicants—i.e., systems for recruitment or selection under Annex III, point 4(a) [Annex III, point 4]—must:

- **Use the system according to the instructions for use** [Art. 26(1)].
- **Monitor its operation** based on those instructions; if the use may present a risk, they must without undue delay inform the provider/distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority and suspend use, and immediately inform the provider (and then the importer/distributor and authorities) of any serious incident [Art. 26(5)].

- **Comply with EU database registration obligations** if they are public authorities or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, and not use a system that has not been registered [Art. 26(8)].

- **Inform the natural persons (e.g., job applicants) that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system** [Art. 26(11)].
- **Perform a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deployment** if they are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, describing the processes, frequency of use, affected categories of persons, specific risks of harm, human oversight measures, and mitigation measures [Art. 27(1)].

question: We are developing an AI tool for a recruitment process that only formats CVs and schedules interviews, without making any hiring decisions. Does this still count as a high-risk AI system?
standalone_question: Does an AI tool used for recruitment that only formats CVs and schedules interviews, without making hiring decisions, count as a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
No. An AI recruitment tool that only formats CVs and schedules interviews—without making or materially influencing hiring decisions—would generally **not** be considered high-risk, provided it does not perform profiling.

Under [Art. 6(3)], an AI system listed in Annex III (such as recruitment tools under [Annex III, point 4(a)]) is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm, “including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making.” This applies where the system is intended to perform a “narrow procedural task” [Art. 6(3)(a)] or a “preparatory task to an assessment” [Art. 6(3)(d)]. [Recital 53] clarifies that narrow procedural tasks include transforming unstructured data into structured data or classifying documents, while preparatory tasks include file handling, indexing, searching, and text processing—activities akin to formatting CVs and scheduling.

However, under [Art. 6(3)], such a system would **always** be high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons. If a provider concludes the system is not high-risk, it must document that assessment before placing it on the market [Art. 6(4)] and register the system in the EU database [Art. 49(2)].

question: We are a local police department and want to use live facial recognition cameras in a public square to verify the identity of a specific suspect. What do we need to do before we can turn the system on, and what if it is an emergency?

It may be deployed only to confirm the identity of a specifically targeted individual, and must take into account the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm if the system were not used, as well as the consequences for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned [Art. 5(2)]. question: Our company is building an AI tool to act as a safety component for managing a city's electricity supply. Would this be considered a high-risk AI system?

question: We are a tech company developing a tool for police departments that predicts whether someone is likely to commit a crime based on their personality traits and online profile. Is this allowed?

answer:
No. Such a tool is prohibited.

[Art. 5(1)(d)] prohibits “the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons in order to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics.” Predicting crime likelihood from personality traits and an online profile falls within this ban. question: We are a private company planning to use biometric data for customer authentication, not for policing. Does the AI Act's ban on certain biometric systems replace our obligations under European data protection rules?

question: As a startup founder looking to test our new AI tool, I'm worried that sandbox procedures might vary wildly from one EU country to another. Will there be uniform rules for applying and participating across the EU?
standalone_question: Are there uniform rules for applying and participating in AI regulatory sandboxes across the EU under the AI Act?
answer: Yes. The Commission is required to adopt implementing acts that specify **common principles** on eligibility and selection criteria, procedures for application, participation, monitoring, exiting and termination, and the terms and conditions applicable to participants [Art. 58(1)]. These rules must ensure that procedures and administrative requirements are **streamlined across the Union** to avoid fragmentation, and that participation in a sandbox established by a Member State is **mutually and uniformly recognised** and carries the same legal effects across the Union [Art. 58(2)(g)]. The implementing acts must also ensure that sandboxes are open to any applying provider who fulfils transparent and fair criteria [Art. 58(2)(a)] and allow broad and equal access [Art. 58(2)(b)], while still supporting flexibility for national competent authorities in establishing and operating their sandboxes [Art. 58(2)(c)].

question: We want to use personal data we already collected for another purpose to train an AI system in a regulatory sandbox that improves health care systems. Is that allowed under the EU AI Act?
standalone_question: We want to use personal data we already collected for another purpose to train an AI system in a regulatory sandbox that improves health care systems. Is that allowed under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, personal data lawfully collected for other purposes may be processed in the AI regulatory sandbox solely for developing, training and testing the AI system, provided all conditions in Article 59(1) are met. Improving health care systems is expressly listed as a substantial public interest area under point (a)(i) [Art. 59(1)(a)].

In addition, the processing is permitted only when: the data are necessary because the relevant requirements cannot be fulfilled with anonymised, synthetic or other non-personal data [Art. 59(1)(b)]; effective monitoring and response mechanisms address high risks to data subjects [Art. 59(1)(c)]; the data are kept in a functionally separate, isolated and protected environment with access limited to authorised persons [Art. 59(1)(d)]; originally collected data are shared only in accordance with Union data protection law and any new personal data created in the sandbox cannot be shared outside it [Art. 59(1)(e)]; the processing does not lead to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects or affect their rights [Art. 59(1)(f)]; and a complete description of the process, rationale and testing results is kept as technical documentation [Art. 59(1)(i)]. This is without prejudice to other Union or national laws governing personal data processing [Art. 59(3)].

question: We are building a high-risk AI system and need to handle our collection data before launching it. What kind of documentation or procedures are we required to have in place for this?
standalone_question: What kind of documentation or procedures are required under the EU AI Act for data collection and handling when building a high-risk AI system?
answer:
Providers must establish data management and governance procedures as part of their quality management system and technical documentation, and retain these records for 10 years.

**Quality management system procedures** must include documented systems and procedures for data management covering "data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention and any other operation regarding the data" performed before placing the system on the market [Art. 17(1)(f)], as well as "systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information" [Art. 17(1)(k)].

**Data governance practices** for training, validation and testing data sets must address: relevant design choices; data collection processes and origin (and original purpose for personal data); data-preparation operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; formulation of assumptions; assessment of availability, quantity and suitability; examination for possible biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights or leading to prohibited discrimination; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases; and identification of data gaps or shortcomings and how to address them [Art. 10(2)]. Data sets must also account for characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use [Art. 10(4)].

**Technical documentation** must be drawn up before the system is placed on the market or put into service, kept up to date, and demonstrate compliance with these requirements [Art. 11(1)].

**Record retention**: the provider must keep the technical documentation and the quality management system documentation at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [Art. 18(1)].

question: As a developer of an AI tool that creates synthetic images, how do technical standards factor into the requirement to make our outputs identifiable as AI-generated?
standalone_question: As a developer of an AI tool that creates synthetic images, how do technical standards factor into the requirement to make our outputs identifiable as AI-generated under the AI Act?

Under the AI Act, technical standards serve as a benchmark for the “generally acknowledged state of the art” that you must consider when designing your marking solution. Article 50(2) requires that your technical solutions for marking synthetic images be “effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible,” and specifies that this feasibility assessment must take into account “the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards” [Art. 50(2)]. Recital 133 confirms that such techniques should be considered “as reflected in the generally acknowledged state of the art” [Recital 133].

question: We are planning to test our AI system in real-world conditions with human participants. Could you explain what informed consent means in this context?
standalone_question: What does informed consent mean in the context of testing an AI system in real-world conditions under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Informed consent means a subject's freely given, specific, unambiguous and voluntary expression of willingness to participate in a particular testing in real-world conditions, after having been informed of all aspects of the testing that are relevant to the subject's decision to participate [Art. 3(59)].

For testing in real-world conditions under Article 60, this consent must be obtained prior to participation and only after the subject has been duly informed with concise, clear, relevant, and understandable information regarding: (a) the nature and objectives of the testing and possible inconvenience; (b) the conditions of testing, including expected duration; (c) their rights and guarantees, in particular the right to refuse and to withdraw at any time without detriment and without justification; (d) arrangements for requesting reversal or disregarding of the AI system's predictions, recommendations or decisions; and (e) the Union-wide unique single identification number and contact details of the provider or legal representative [Art. 61(1)]. The informed consent shall be dated and documented, and a copy shall be given to the subject or their legal representative [Art. 61(2)]. Subjects may withdraw their informed consent at any time without detriment and without justification, and may request the immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data [Art. 60(5)].

Yes, in principle. Under the AI Act, deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text “published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest” must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated [Art. 50(4)]. A news blog on local government policies falls within informing the public on matters of public interest, and Recital 134 confirms a similar disclosure obligation for AI-generated or manipulated text in that context [Recital 134].

The obligation does not apply where the AI-generated content “has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content,” or where use is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes [Art. 50(4)]. The disclosure must be provided clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first exposure [Art. 50(5)].

This is not legal advice.

question: Our company is an AI operator facing a potential penalty. What factors are taken into account when determining whether to issue an administrative fine and how much it will be?
standalone_question: What factors are taken into account when determining whether to issue an administrative fine under the EU AI Act and how much it will be?
answer:
When deciding whether to impose an administrative fine and determining its amount, the relevant authorities take into account the following:

**For operators and notified bodies**, all relevant circumstances shall be considered, including: the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences (taking into account the purpose of the AI system, the number of affected persons and the level of damage suffered); whether fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities for the same infringement or by other authorities for related infringements; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; aggravating or mitigating factors such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided; the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities; the degree of responsibility based on technical and organisational measures implemented; how the infringement became known (in particular whether the operator notified it); the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any action taken to mitigate harm to affected persons [Art. 99(7)].

**For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies**, due regard is given to: the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences; the degree of responsibility based on technical and organisational measures; actions taken to mitigate damage; cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor (including compliance with previous measures); similar previous infringements; how the infringement became known (including notification by the entity); and the entity's annual budget [Art. 100(1)].

**For providers of general-purpose AI models**, regard is had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, taking due account of proportionality and appropriateness, as well as commitments made under Article 93(3) or relevant codes of practice [Art. 101(1)].

Regarding the amounts: non-compliance with the prohibitions in Article 5 is subject to fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover [Art. 99(3)]; non-compliance with specified obligations of operators and notified bodies (Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33, 34, 50) up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of turnover [Art. 99(4)]; for Union institutions, Article 5 violations up to EUR 1 500 000 [Art. 100(2)] and other non-compliance up to EUR 750 000 [Art. 100(3)]; and for general-purpose AI model providers, fines not exceeding 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher [Art. 101(1

They also look at the operator's degree of responsibility and cooperation, whether the infringement was intentional or negligent, any actions taken to mitigate harm, and any previous fines or financial benefits gained.

question: Our company is developing an AI tool that creates synthetic text content for blogs. What technical requirements must we meet for the generated outputs?
standalone_question: What technical requirements must our company meet for generated outputs of an AI tool that creates synthetic text content for blogs under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
Under the AI Act, if your company is the **provider** of an AI system that generates synthetic text content, the outputs must be **marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated** [Art. 50(2)]. Your technical solutions must be **effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible**, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the content type, implementation costs, and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as reflected in relevant technical standards [Art. 50(2)]. This marking obligation does **not** apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or where use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences [Art. 50(2)]. Recital 133 confirms these techniques should be sufficiently reliable, interoperable, effective and robust, and may include watermarks, metadata, cryptographic provenance methods, logging, or fingerprints [Recital 133].

If your company is the **deployer** and the blog text is **published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest**, you must additionally **disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated**, unless the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility [Art. 50(4)].

question: Our lab is building a versatile AI model for internal prototyping activities before we ever release it. Does it count as a general-purpose AI model under the rules?
standalone_question: Does our lab's versatile AI model built for internal prototyping activities before any release count as a general-purpose AI model under the EU AI Act?
answer:
No — if the model is used only for internal prototyping before any release, it does **not** count as a general-purpose AI model: the definition expressly excludes “AI models that are used for research, development or prototyping activities before they are placed on the market” [Art. 3(63)], and the Regulation also does not apply to research, testing or development activity “prior to their being placed on the market or put into service,” except real-world testing [Art. 2(8)]. The same intent is stated in [Recital 97]: the definition “should not cover AI models used before their placing on the market for the sole purpose of research, development and prototyping activities.”

If it is later released, it could count if it “displays significant generality” and can “competently perform[] a wide range of distinct tasks” [Art. 3(63)]. This is not legal advice.

question: We manufacture protective systems for potentially explosive atmospheres, and our new AI-based safety component must undergo an external conformity assessment. Would that AI system be classified as high-risk?
standalone_question: Would our AI-based safety component for protective systems in potentially explosive atmospheres be classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act, requiring an external conformity assessment?
answer:
Yes. An AI-based safety component for protective systems intended for use in potentially explosive atmospheres is classified as high-risk where both conditions in [Art. 6(1)] are met: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. [Recital 50] expressly lists “equipment and protective systems intended for use in potentially explosive atmospheres” among the products covered where a third-party conformity assessment applies.

As for external assessment: for such high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure required under that legislation, and only the derogations established in that legislation apply [Art. 43(3)] [Art. 46(7)]. The product manufacturer is considered the provider of the high-risk AI system in the circumstances set out in [Art. 25(3)]. This is not legal advice.

question: As a provider of a general-purpose AI model, do I need to include information about how we detect identifiable biases in our technical documentation?
standalone_question: As a provider of a general-purpose AI model, do I need to include information about how we detect identifiable biases in our technical documentation under the AI Act?
answer:
Yes — as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, the technical documentation you must draw up and keep up-to-date under Article 53(1)(a) must contain, at a minimum, the information in Annex XI [Art. 53(1)]. For all providers of general-purpose AI models, Annex XI, Section 1 requires a detailed description of the development process, including “information on the data used for training, testing and validation … how the data was obtained and selected as well as all other measures to detect the unsuitability of data sources and methods to detect identifiable biases, where applicable” [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2]. This is part of the information “as appropriate to the size and risk profile of the model” under Annex XI, Section 1 [Annex XI, Section 1].

This is not legal advice.

question: My company is preparing compliance paperwork for a new AI model. Do we need to include the training time, and what other training-related details must we provide?
standalone_question: What training-related details, such as training time, must a company provide for a new AI model under the EU AI Act?
answer:
For a **general-purpose AI model**, the provider must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation that includes, at a minimum, the following training-related details: information on the **data used for training, testing and validation** (type, provenance, curation methodologies, number of data points, scope, main characteristics, how the data was obtained and selected, and measures to detect unsuitability of data sources and identifiable biases); the **computational resources used** (e.g. number of floating point operations), **training time**, and other relevant details related to the training; and the **known or estimated energy consumption** of the model (where unknown, this may be based on information about computational resources used) [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2]. This documentation must be provided to the AI Office and national competent authorities upon request [Art. 53(1)].

Providers must also make available to downstream AI system providers information that includes, at a minimum, **information on the data used for training, testing and validation**, including its type, provenance and curation methodologies [Annex XII].

For **high-risk AI systems**, the provided excerpts require that they be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet specific quality criteria, but they do not specify the same granular training details such as training time [Art. 10(1)].

question: What do we need to explain about our software components in the technical documentation for our AI system?
standalone_question: What do we need to explain about our software components in the technical documentation for our AI system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
For a high-risk AI system, the technical documentation must include **a description of the system architecture explaining how software components build on or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing**, together with the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate the AI system [Annex IV, point 2]. You must also describe **how the AI system interacts with, or can be used to interact with, hardware or software that is not part of the AI system itself** [Annex IV, point 1].

If your AI system is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, the documentation must similarly contain **a detailed description of the system architecture explaining how software components build or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing** [Annex XI, Section 2, points 1–3].
